scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1779, Gennaro Magri redefined the 'grotesque' dancer not as a buffoon, but as a 'vortex of force' capable of multiple-turn pirouettes on one foot that put courtly amateurs to shame.
This is Grotesque dance. 18th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The genre became clearly differentiated in the 18th century but has roots in the 16th and 17th centuries as an anti-masque or comic interlude.
In the court of Louis XIII, the Duke of Nemours devised grotesque sequences for the 'entrée de ballet,' a format of loosely connected tableaux.
While some early performers were chosen for physical deformities, the Italian tradition eventually elevated the form into a display of high athleticism.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally intended to amuse and entertain spectators or patrons as a contrast to serious courtly themes, it served as a 'comic' or 'lighthearted' counterpoint to the noble dance.
It represents the body as a site of concentrated kinetic energy rather than just aesthetic beauty.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers use 'false positions' (inwardly turned) or 'Spanish positions' (neutral) instead of the standard French turnout.
The technique involves 'vortex of force' kinetic principles, where energy is concentrated and released.
Key movements include pirouettes on one foot for as many turns as possible, wrapping steps, and complex airborne beats (cabrioles).
Watch for Salto dell'impiccato, Pirouette on one foot, Cabrioles.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is typically comic or lighthearted to suit buffoons and Commedia dell'arte characters.
Notable compositions include works by André Campra and the 'Dorcon's dance' section in Maurice Ravel's Daphnis et Chloé.
Listen for the Orchestral instruments of the 18th century.

narration: Grotesque dance was performed in theatrical settings, including royal courts and public theaters.
Costumes often represented buffoons or specific Commedia dell'arte archetypes, designed to facilitate the high-impact jumps and turns of the style.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Gennaro Magri is the central figure, whose 1779 treatise defended the style.
Other notable dancers include Margrethe Schall and John D'Auban, as well as the Duke of Nemours who choreographed for Louis XIII.
The Italian tradition (ballo grottesco) is noted for its extreme virtuosity and athleticism compared to the more character-driven French 'danse grotesque.'
It evolved from the anti-masque and the 17th-century 'entrée de ballet' into a formal category of theatrical dance that influenced later character dance in classical ballet.
